headline: Your hand bones
body: Growth plate senescence runs earlier in smaller bones than larger ones.
punch: Which is a problem, because bone age is read from a hand X-ray.

headline: Bone age
body: A single figure describing how far along your skeleton is. One value, whole body, read from a radiograph of the hand and wrist.
punch: Skeletons don't work on one clock.

headline: The finding
body: Growth plate senescence — declining proliferation, hypertrophy and cell depletion — occurs earlier in metacarpals and phalanges than in femurs and tibias.
punch: Small bones start finishing while long bones are still going.

headline: Which is exactly
body: The bones read for bone age are the ones furthest along. The bones that determine your height are the ones with more time left.
punch: You're measuring the finished work to estimate the unfinished.

headline: Human imaging
body: MRI of 958 people aged 14 to 21 found fusion timing varied by skeletal site within the same individual — wrist, knee and ankle did not close together.
punch: One person, several different closure dates.

headline: It also found
body: Pubertal stage correlated with fusion far better than chronological age — supporting hormonal exposure, not time elapsed, as the direct driver.
punch: Correlation coefficients around 0.5 to 0.6 for stage, weaker for age.

headline: And a two-year gap
body: Complete fusion occurred roughly two years earlier in girls than boys, across every site measured.
punch: Same species, same sites, systematically different schedules.

headline: What to take from it
body: A single bone age number is a useful clinical estimate and a poor description of reality. Different bones are on different schedules, and the one you measure isn't the one you care about.
punch: Useful estimate. Not a physical fact.

headline: It's never over
body: Real mechanisms, real citations, no protocols.
